Return raw JSON only. Do not use Markdown fences, introductory or concluding prose, comments, or any text outside the JSON. Do not invent enum values. Return exactly one row for every requested monitor, with no omitted or duplicated monitor IDs. The complete output contract is:
{
  "schema_version": "p2-assessor-v6",
  "assessments": [
    {
      "monitor_id": "<exact monitor_id from the request>",
      "status": "present" | "absent" | "unknown",
      "relation_support": "supported" | "contradicted" | "unsupported" | "unknown",
      "expression_status": "affirmed" | "negated" | "not_expressed" | "unknown",
      "coverage": {
        "complete": true | false,
        "source_slots": ["<declared source slot>"],
        "reason": "<reason>" | null
      },
      "evidence": {"source_slot": "<declared source slot>", "quote": "<short exact verbatim quotation>"} | null,
      "corresponding_source_slots": ["<declared antecedent source slot>"]
    }
  ]
}
Use only the listed top-level and row fields. The schema_version must be exactly p2-assessor-v6. For status=present, coverage must name covered declared source slots and evidence must contain a non-empty exact quotation from its source_slot. Status=present means the proposition is addressed by the available required sources; it does not by itself mean the proposition is affirmed. For status=present, coverage.complete must be true and source_slots must include every available required source slot; an unavailable required source means status=unknown. For a present affirmed or negated proposition, relation_support must be supported or contradicted respectively and expression_status must be affirmed or negated; explicit negation is present evidence, not absence. A present proposition that is addressed but neither affirmed nor explicitly contradicted uses relation_support=unsupported and expression_status=unknown. Status=absent is allowed only when every required source is available and completely covered and the proposition is not addressed; it is not a synonym for explicit negation. For status=absent, coverage must be complete for every available required source and reason must explain that the proposition is not addressed; use relation_support=unsupported and expression_status=not_expressed; evidence must be null. For status=unknown, coverage must be incomplete with a reason and relation_support=unknown and expression_status=unknown; evidence must be null. Never use not_expressed for explicit negation. Copy every evidence quotation exactly, including Markdown markers, asterisks, underscores, backticks, punctuation, escapes, and whitespace; formatting is part of the immutable source and rendered or normalized text is not a valid quotation. Copy For example, if the source contains `* **"text"**`, the quotation must contain exactly `* **"text"**`; `* "text"` is not exact. monitor IDs and source slots exactly from the request. Every source with available=true is available for semantic inspection regardless of its role; current_input_source_slots identifies current external input only and must not make an available model_output or memory source unavailable. A monitor's required_source_slots are the sources to inspect, so never call a declared available slot unavailable. Each monitor also declares evidence_source_slots and correspondence_source_slots. Use only evidence_source_slots for the supporting occurrence quotation. Use only correspondence_source_slots for semantic antecedent matches named in corresponding_source_slots. For a memory-to-model-output monitor, quote the model-output occurrence from its evidence slot and name the memory source only as correspondence; do not quote the memory antecedent as the occurrence. Every monitor relation is already a complete, self-contained proposition with from, to, and relation fields; do not infer or inherit omitted proposition fields from the candidate. Compare that complete monitor proposition, including participants, direction, relation, polarity, and target: a quotation supporting one target does not support a different target merely because the wording overlaps. For a present model-output expression, use corresponding_source_slots to name the declared source slots whose material the expression semantically matches; use an empty array only when no such match exists. Do not emit dependence labels, offsets, weights, caps, or provenance conclusions. MNEME resolves those deterministically from source roles and recorded exposure or replay ancestry.

      "source_id": "2253ee79-4787-4b88-9654-d39a3a2c39ce",
      "text": "I like the idea of using old bottles for wicking, but I'm not sure how long the water would last. Do you think it would be enough for a weekend?"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s1",
      "source_id": "a8e1e388-304e-4dc4-a51e-28a1551c4a97",
      "text": "Actually, it depends on the size of your pots and how quickly the weather is drying them out. For a typical weekend (say, 48 hours), a single bottle can often provide enough water for a small cluster of plants. \n\nIf you are worried about the plants dying, you might need a few extra \"saturator\" bottles. If you are in an extremely hot area, one bottle might only last half a day.\n\nTo make it reliable for a full weekend, you might need to:\n\n*   **Combine two:** Use one large, empty 2-liter bottle (or two smaller ones) per pot, filled with water and placed *next to* the pot, to ensure the water level remains consistent.\n*   **The \"Double-Up\" approach:** If you have a larger plant, you might need two or even three \"saturators\" per plant.\n\nIf you are worried about a hot, dry weekend, it's best to over-water slightly rather than risk a complete die-off. If your plants are in a very dry, hot environment, you might want to use two water-holding systems per plant instead of just one."
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s2",
      "source_id": "a9b1d4c5-c5e2-45b8-bd5f-c0a9db63a17f",
      "text": "That's reassuring. I guess I'll try the double-up approach with a couple of pots, but I'm still worried about the soil drying out too fast. Do you think I should add something to the soil to help retain moisture?"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s3",
      "source_id": "74c4d300-cd7e-44c2-928e-2c9c885bb463",
      "text": "Adding something to the soil to help retain moisture is a great idea! Since you are looking for a reliable, hands-off solution, you have a few \"household material\" options you can use:\n\n1.  **Peat Moss or Peat Moss:** If you have access to it, mixing a small amount of peat moss into the top layer of your soil will significantly increase its water retention capacity, making it \"hold\" moisture for longer.\n2.  **Coir or Compost:** If you have any old, uncomposted garden material or even some plain compost, mixing this into the soil can also help retain humidity better than just pure sand or dirt.\n3.  **Mulch Layer:** The best *external* material to add would be a layer of **mulch**—things like dried grass clippings, dry leaves, or even straw placed *on top* of the soil. This acts like a blanket, preventing the hot sun from evaporating the water too quickly.\n4.  **Water-Retaining Polymers:** If you can find some kind of \"super-absorbent polymer\" (like the type used in some industrial \"sponge\" products), adding a small amount to the soil can help absorb and release water very slowly."
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "external",
      "slot": "s4",
      "source_id": "c9af8ba1-df9d-4160-891b-45fddc4373a4",
      "text": "I'll try the mulch layer first—it sounds simple enough. But if that doesn't work, I might need to look for peat moss. Do you think it's possible to overdo the moisture retention? I don't want the roots to sit in water."
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s5",
      "source_id": "86bb2225-fad4-4e4c-a87e-5f10ab8a3b97",
      "text": "Actually, you absolutely can, but you should be careful. Over-watering is one of the biggest risks when trying to keep a plant alive!\n\nInstead of trying to force a super high amount of moisture, a better strategy is to create a \"slow-release\" system. Since you're worried about the water drying out fast, try these specific techniques:\n\n1.  **Water-Saturating Soil:** Instead of just adding more water, try to build up your soil composition. If you are using **sand or soil** as a base, it’s often best to mix in some **compost** (like a high-quality, high-quality organic compost) to give the soil structure more \"body\" and ability to hold onto water better than pure sand alone.\n2.  **In-Soil Dampening:** If you are using a 2-liter bottle as a reservoir, instead of letting the water just sit in the pot, you could potentially use a **\"Wicking\" system** where the water bottle *sits in contact with* the soil surface rather than just being near it. This is how \"self-watering\" systems work—they are much better at consistent maintenance.\n\nRegarding your concern about over-watering"
    }
